newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - New broker ruffles City of London's morning ritual.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New broker ruffles City of London's morning ritual.

text.p: Mornings in the City of London may soon never be the same again.
Doubts have been raised about a key fixture of the financial district's daily routine -- the morning meeting.

For years, analysts and traders in each of London's broking houses have held early morning gatherings to decide the day's sales pitch to clients. Analysts address the meeting one by one, often through a microphone in the centre of the dealing room, passing on news, research and share tips to their sales team.

This information is then relayed to the brokerage's fund manager clients, who -- if all goes according to plan -- will respond by buying or selling shares, generating the business which keeps traders and analysts in their jobs.
From the oldest blue-blood broking houses to the newest foreign-owned operations, the morning meeting has become a ritual in London's securities houses -- except one.
Schroder Securities, newly-formed broking arm of blue-chip British merchant bank Schroders Plc, has said it will not hold daily morning meetings among its British sales and research team.
Philip Augar, head of Schroder Securities, says he believes such meetings create only "claptrap and noise".

Rather than bombarding fund managers with the daily output of morning meetings, Augar says he wants his analysts to produce a lower volume but a higher quality of ideas. Clients will only be called with new, original research, he says.
As a relatively small operation, Schroder Securities needs less business to cover its costs than bigger rivals and Augar says this allows the firm to dispense with morning meetings.
"We have the luxury of not having to create ideas constantly simply to churn shares," he says.
RETHINKING RESEARCH
Many fund managers would be delighted if brokers rang them less.

"We would welcome fewer phone calls and better quality phone calls," the head of British equities at one major insurance company told Reuters. "We fund managers are continually fighting against the white noise which comes out of brokers."

Fund managers are growing increasingly choosy about the service they receive from securities houses. Many now have their own in-house analysts and conduct their own company visits. And as real-time financial information becomes more readily available, the need for brokers to pass on news is dwindling.
As a result, more and more broker research is being ignored.

The 1997 Reuters survey of research on larger European companies found that 33 percent of fund management groups are now spending less time reading and listening to securities houses' research, compared with eight percent the previous year.
Of the fund managers surveyed, 47 percent said they were using fewer brokers for research.

"It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that much of this broker research is being squeezed out by the development of in-house research by the fund management groups themselves," said Tempest Consultants, who compiled the survey.
In this climate, fund managers are demanding more than short-term share tips and news from their brokers.

"We're continually investigating ways to get brokers to call fewer times and to make their comments more value-added when they do call. People are looking for detailed, original research, not off-the-cuff ideas," the fund manager said.
"Our investment decisions would normally have rather more thought behind them than simply BZW are a buyer so I'll take a quarter of a million shares'."
EXCHANGING IDEAS
So is the sun setting on the morning meeting? Most brokers are quick to spring to They admit that the nature of

research is changing and that clients want detailed, in-depth research which the morning meeting cannot provide. But they say the gatherings were never intended to produce quality research, but instead provide an invaluable forum for exchanging ideas, news and rumours.
"They are an excellent tool for analysts, economists, salesmen and traders to get together and exchange thoughts," said Richard Jeffrey, head of research at Charterhouse Tilney.
"Getting people together is beneficial in itself, and from time to time they produce observations which are extremely useful," he said.
"An analyst might say something, a salesperson might respond, and it adds value to both their jobs."
And despite their grumbles, most fund managers are reluctant to write off the morning meeting altogether.

"It's stretching it to say that morning meeting comments are useless, although I would not expect fund managers to be actively dealing on the back of them," the insurance company fund manager told Reuters.

"I look at morning meetings as a way of transmitting news items and changes in recommendations, which I feed into an investment process which involves further work, analysis and discussion, which may lead to an investment decision," he said.
So for the time being, analysts are unlikely to get an extra hour in bed in the morning. Most brokerages have no plans to abandon their morning gatherings.
"It's missing the point to complain that morning meetings don't generate in-depth insights every day. That's not what they're for," said the head of sales at a major U.S. investment bank in London.
"Show us a better way of exchanging information and keeping people informed and we'll use it," he said. "Until then, we'll stick with the morning meeting."
